newsitem.title: INDIA: ACC sees India cement growth at 8.0 pct.
newsitem.headline: ACC sees India cement growth at 8.0 pct.

text.p: Growth in Indian cement demand would be around 8.0 percent in 1996/97 (April-March), a top official of the country's largest cement firm said.

"The cement industry would record growth of at least 8.0 percent this year against 12 percent last year," Subrato Ganguly, vice chairman of Associated Cement Companies (ACC) told reporters, late on Wednesday.
He said annual growth in the past has been around 8.0 percent except for 1995/96 which was an exceptionally good year for the industry.
"We (the industry) would be producing around 70 million tonnes for the year ending March 1997," Ganguly said. "It's a great achievement in a commodity product," he said.
Supply and demand are generally about the same in India's cement sector, industry sources said.
Ganguly said the industry maintained the 12 percent growth from April to June but sales and despatches began slowing in mid-August. The growth in September was down to 10 percent.
"This had serious results in selling price," he said. The company attributed the dipping sales to a slowdown in economy.
The downslide was most severe in northern India, where prices fell by 15 percent in the last six months, he said.
Ganguly said ACC's variable costs within its plants jumped 10 percent in the first half of 1996/97 from previous levels, while recovery in cement prices was much lower.
On Tuesday, ACC announced a steep fall in first half net profit to 550.5 million rupees, down from 1.25 billion rupees during the year-ago period.
The company, part of the Tata Group, India's largest business house, blames unprecedented cost increases for its poor performance.
"Costs have gone up significantly," Ganguly said.
He said delivered price of coal jumped 15 percent during the first half. "We don't think we've seen the end (of price increases by state-run Coal India Ltd," he said.
Power cost 4.10 rupees per unit in the central Indian state of Madhya Pradesh, India's cement bowl, and even at such a high price power supply was erratic.
"Freight (costs) has worsened to an extent unimaginable," Ganguly said. ACC is India's largest private transporter, moving over 14 million tonnes a year, he said.
Three years ago, ACC was dependant on railways for 70 percent of its requirements. Today, it has fallen to 50 percent, road traffic accounting for the balance.
"Road is worse - it is diesel-led and mafia-led," he said, referring to recent price increase in diesel and truckers unions which dictate freight rates.
Ganguly said ACC's new cement plants were as efficient as some of its competitors who built their plants in recent years.
"We are not saying we are the best - we have the disadvantage of history, with the largest share of (old technology) wet process plants," ACC managing director T.M.M. Nambiar said.
ACC has an ongoing 20 billion rupee capital expenditure programme, of which 88 percent is devoted to cement.

"ACC intends to maintain its leadership by implementing expansions at key locations at lower than industry costs and also to invest in distribution and infrastructure to ensure optimal use of capacity," the firm said in a statement.
